ai_technology: AlphaFold2-Multimer; molecular dynamics and electrophysiological tests

evidence.ai_role: Learned multimer structure predictions identify tail conformations and candidate gating contacts that are checked experimentally.
evidence.tested: Within-study electrophysiology of predicted channel constructs and interface changes, supported by molecular dynamics.
evidence.unknown: Sequence-wide structural generalization is predicted; model confidence is not experimental confirmation of every bacterial channel or human-channel mechanism.

organization: University of Texas at Austin; Flatiron Institute; Max Planck Institute of Biophysics

source_review.scope: Primary full manuscript Methods, Results, validation protocol and limitations independently reviewed.

summary: A preprint combined AlphaFold2-Multimer predictions, molecular dynamics and electrophysiology to study a sodium channel from the marine bacterium Ruegeria pomeroyi. Predicted tail conformations suggested contacts that stabilize channel opening and reduce temperature sensitivity; targeted substitutions altered temperature responses in the predicted contexts. The study argues that the tail modulates gating rather than serving as a temperature sensor itself. Predictions across more than 800 bacterial sequences suggest broader conservation, but those channels were not all experimentally tested. The result concerns bacterial-channel biophysics, not a demonstrated mechanism in human neurons.
title: AlphaFold-guided tests link bacterial channel tails to temperature gating
